bib.title: Climbing towards NLU: On Meaning, Form, and Understanding in the Age of Data
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2020), pages 5185-5198

question: Can a system trained only on linguistic form (string prediction) learn meaning, and how should the field talk about and evaluate large language models given the answer?
hypothesis: A system trained only on form has a priori no way to learn meaning, so claims that large LMs 'understand' language are overclaims.
contributions: A working definition of form, conventional meaning and communicative intent, with 'understand' as retrieving intent i given expression e
Thought experiments (octopus test, Java, English plus unlinked photos) showing what is missing from form-only training data
A set of 'hillclimbing diagnostics' for task design and reporting

results.claim: Central thesis: language modeling on form alone cannot in principle lead to learning of meaning.
results.setup: Theoretical argument; 'language model' means any system trained only on string prediction over characters, words or sentences, sequential or not.
results.quote:
We argue that the language modeling task, be-
cause it only uses form as training data, cannot in
principle lead to learning of meaning.

results.claim: Meaning is defined as the relation M subset of E x I between expressions and communicative intents; understanding is retrieving i given e.
results.setup: Working definition; conventional meaning is a separate relation C subset of E x S.
results.quote:
Given this
deﬁnition of meaning, we can now use understand
to refer to the process of retrieving i given e.

results.claim: Octopus test: a statistical-pattern learner that only sees form can imitate social chit-chat but fails once the exchange needs grounding in the world (coconut catapult, bear emergency); the human partner does the work of attributing meaning.
results.setup: Thought experiment, octopus O taps a cable between English speakers A and B; weak Turing test.
results.quote:
It is absolutely conceivable that A accepts
this reply as meaningful — but only because A does
all the work in attributing meaning to O’s response.

results.claim: Constrained thought experiments: an LM trained on all Github Java with no bytecode, compiler or input/output pairs cannot be expected to execute programs; an English LM plus unlinked photos cannot answer questions about a photo.
results.setup: Thought experiments with unlimited training time and any LM type.
results.quote:
a sys-
tem trained only on the form of Java or English has no way learn their
respective meaning relations.
results.note: Source text reads 'has no way learn' (sic).

results.claim: Children do not acquire language from passive exposure; learning relies on joint attention and intersubjectivity.
results.source: Snow et al. 1976; Kuhl 2007; Baldwin 1995; Tomasello and Farrar 1986; Brooks and Meltzoff 2005
results.setup: Language-acquisition literature; Kuhl: English-learning infants learn Mandarin phonemic distinctions from brief interaction with a speaker but not from TV or radio; Baldwin: toddlers aged 18-20 months do not pick up labels uttered from behind a screen.
results.quote:
Human children do not learn meaning from
form alone and we should not expect machines to
do so either.

results.claim: BERT's performance on the Argument Reasoning Comprehension Task falls back to chance when adversarial examples negating one piece mirror the lexical cues for each label.
results.quote:
falls back to chance if the dataset is modiﬁed
by adding adversarial examples

results.claim: BERT's MNLI performance relies on syntactic overlap heuristics; on a dataset designed to frustrate them it falls significantly below chance.
results.setup: English MNLI (Williams et al. 2018), BERT; heuristics are overlap of full constituents, subsequences or bags of words.
results.quote:
BERT’s performance
falls to signiﬁcantly below chance.

results.claim: GPT-2 774M, prompted with a bear-and-sticks plea, gave five unhelpful completions (no cherry-picking); it captures which activity words co-occur with bears and sticks, not what to do.
results.setup: GPT-2 774M via talktotransformer.com, accessed 2019/12/09; prompt 'Robinson cried out, ... The survivalist said, "Here's what you can do.'; first five random completions; judgement is the authors' own reading, no scoring rubric.
results.quote:
The ﬁrst ﬁve random com-
pletions (no cherrypicking) were as follows.
results.note: The count 0 of 5 is inferred from the authors' statement that none of the completions would be helpful.

results.claim: GPT-2 completions of 'Three plus five equals' were incoherent text; the authors judge arithmetic-in-language beyond GPT-2 and any pure LM.
results.setup: GPT-2, same procedure as Appendix A, five responses; answers begin seven, six, (none), ten, five, none is eight.
results.quote:
show that
this problem is beyond the current capability of
GPT-2, and, we would argue, any pure LM.
results.note: Tiny anecdotal sample; exact GPT-2 size for Appendix B not stated (footnote 11 gives 774M for Appendix A).

results.claim: Training signals that declare form-meaning links (NLI labels, control codes, tl;dr) go beyond pure form, so the thesis does not rule out such systems learning some semantic relations.
results.setup: Discussion of counterarguments, Sec 9; also Java unit tests as weak interaction data requiring a learner built to interpret them.
results.quote:
Similarly, control codes, or tokens
like tl;dr, have been used to prompt large LMs to
perform summarization and other tasks

results.claim: The amount of form is irrelevant to the thesis: the octopus can observe indefinitely and the Java corpus is unbounded, but responding to novel intents would need unbounded memorised stimulus-response pairs.
results.setup: Counterargument 'there is so much form out there'.
results.quote:
How much form can be observed is not
relevant to our point

results.claim: If unsupervised MT trained only with an LM objective on monolingual corpora reached supervised accuracy, it would contradict the thesis, implying accurate MT does not require understanding.
results.setup: Stated as a conditional, not an observed result.
results.quote:
this
would seem contradict our conclusion that meaning
cannot be learned from form.

results.claim: Five hillclimbing diagnostics: ask top-down questions with humility, know task limits (a system beating inter-annotator agreement probably exploits artifacts), value careful new tasks (DROP), evaluate across tasks (SuperGLUE), analyse errors and successes.
results.setup: Sec 8.2 best practices for evaluation of claims about meaning.
results.quote:
If a system does better on such a task than the
inter-annotator agreement,9 the task probably has
statistical artifacts that do not represent meaning.

limits: Position paper: no experiments except two anecdotal GPT-2 runs in the appendices (5 completions each, no scoring).

The argument is about models trained only on form (LM objective); the authors state it does not apply to downstream systems trained on tasks that carry semantic relations, nor to LMs given grounding data.
Authors concede that unsupervised MT matching supervised MT, or learners equipped to interpret unit tests, would complicate the conclusion.
Predates instruction tuning, RLHF, multimodal and tool-using LLMs; the GPT-2 appendix examples reflect 2019 models (774M). Later systems are not addressed.
Definition of 'meaning' is a chosen working definition; the authors say defining it is notoriously hard.
practices: Use precise language about model abilities; define 'understand', 'comprehend' as technical terms if not meant in the human-analogous sense (Sec 2, 10).
Cultivate humility towards language and ask top-down questions (Sec 8.2).
Be aware of the limits of artificial and crowdsourced tasks such as bAbI, SQuAD and SNLI (Sec 8.2).
Value and support the careful creation of new tasks such as DROP (Sec 8.2).
Evaluate models of meaning across tasks, e.g. SuperGLUE (Sec 8.2).
Analyse both errors and successes, with healthy skepticism of results that look too good to be true (Sec 8.2).

terms.definition: any observable realization of language: marks on a page, pixels or bytes in a digital representation of text, or movements of the articulators
the relation between the form and something external to language; formally M subset of E x I, pairs of expressions and the communicative intents they can evoke
the purpose a speaker has in using language, such as conveying information, requesting action or socialising
what is constant across all possible contexts of use of an expression; relation C subset of E x S
the process of retrieving communicative intent i given expression e
any system trained only on the task of string prediction, whether over characters, words or sentences, and sequentially or not
thought experiment of a hyper-intelligent octopus tapping a cable between two English speakers and later impersonating one; a weak Turing test
Harnad (1990): the impossibility of learning the meanings of Chinese words from Chinese dictionary definitions alone
